doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Solo for Lou Rawls film song under Don Costa that went unused
summary: Recording a solo at MGM for a Rawls movie song, and learning that work for hire can be discarded.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You’ve heard of this? Oh. Well anyway there were several of these movies. One of them, this particular one, was called “The Soul of Nigger Charlie,” it was a western, right, in which the hero was a black man who had problems. Okay. So there were several songs that Lou was going to record and one of them was called “Sunshine Day.” Well this was arranged by a guy named Don Costa, who was a very well-known musical director and arranger for the movies, and it was done at MGM studios in Los Angeles, and I was brought in as a guitar soloist, right? So again, they were going to do doing the chart and then the section in there where I had to do some solo work. All right. So they bring in my stuff, and it’s next to, oh I can’t remember who the guys were but it’d be people like Larry Carlton and, you know, all these famous studio musicians are there, Tommy Tedesco, and all these guys would be there, and then it would be this guitar player, so they’d move over or then they’d go in the other room or something like that, and there was a big orchestra with the movie showing up on the screen and all this, and so we go through and we play the thing and we did a couple of takes, and it was fine, and Costa — oh and after I played my solos they would listen to the playback and Costa comes back up and he steps on this little podium and he says “that’s a wrap. And I want to thank the guitar player here for putting on that thing” — and the whole orchestra starts to applaud. And I said oh my God, I’m getting applause from the studio orchestra, isn’t that cool? So I can’t wait to hear this thing in a movie. So a few weeks later we’re playing in Boston and there on the movie theater, the marquee, “The Soul of Nigger Charlie.” Oh great, I’m going to go hear myself in a movie. So I went to the movie theater and there it is, and I begin to hear my opening lick [scats] that’s me playing that guitar part. And when it come to my big solo, they had placed girls’ voices over my solo, so you could kind of hear a little faint guitar in the background, but you heard girls singing [scats]. So the © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -21-

lesson learned there is that once you’ve done a work for hire, they can do whatever they want with it. They can use it, they can not use it, whatever. So I said jeez, it was a good solo, wasn’t it? It was a good experience, it just didn’t come out in public that way. So I got myself on the movie screen and on the radio.
